transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-06
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood CSM), Sara (Edenfield IT), Daniel (Edenfield Legal), Maya (Edenfield DPO), Tom (Edenfield Platform)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Edenfield is evaluating Redwood for customer-facing wealth-advisor tools and some internal automation. Key constraints: EU/UK residency for EEA customers, selective HIPAA scope for small set of medical records tied to health benefits for employees, strict logging/retention rules from financial regulator, and need for KMS customer-managed keys. They want to understand Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs, how logs are redacted or segmented, and what contract/legal artifacts Redwood can provide. Next: send security pack, schedule SE deep dive and agree on pilot metrics.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: All right folks, thanks for joining. Looks like we have everyone. This is Avery from Redwood, AE on the account. Marco and Priya are our SEs, Liam from CSM as well. Could we do quick intros?
[00:09] Sara Whitman: Hi hi, Sara here, head of IT at Edenfield. We're the platform team, we own infra and integrations.
[00:13] Daniel Park: Daniel, legal counsel. I'll be focused on contract and data processing terms.
[00:17] Maya Iqbal: Maya, data privacy officer — GDPR lead, also covering some UK regulator work.
[00:21] Tom Ruiz: Tom, platform engineer, I'll be the point on technical feasibility.
[00:24] Marco Silva: Marco here, I'll try to keep questions practical, talk about topology and logs.
[00:28] Avery Chen: Cool. High level — Edenfield, you're building advisor-facing flows that will generate recommendations and internal automation for client onboarding — is that right, Sara?
[00:37] Sara Whitman: Yeah that's the gist. A mix of client-facing generation and internal scoring. We have to ensure customer data doesn't leave EU for EU customers, and for some regulated products we need an auditable trail but with PII masked.
[00:47] Priya Nair: When you say auditable trail, is the requirement to keep raw prompts or only metadata? Curious what the regulator wants.
[00:54] Maya Iqbal: Financial regulator wants a full audit trail for advice decisions for up to 7 years. But we are pushing to mask or pseudonymize PII in the raw text. We need proof-of-processing and chain-of-custody.
[01:07] Marco Silva: Got it. How many regions are we talking for residency? EU only, or also UK, Switzerland, etc?
[01:12] Sara Whitman: EU plus UK for sure. Potentially Switzerland depending on client. No US residency for EU customer data.
[01:19] Avery Chen: Two things we should talk through: deployment modes (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and logging/Audit controls. Quick primer — hosted keeps data in our managed region and is fastest to get started; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and better tenancy isolation; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives full control of networking and keys. For residency we can pin regions and apply routing policies.
[01:36] Tom Ruiz: If we need to ensure data never crosses out of EU, is Hosted ok? We've seen hosted offerings that still call outbound services in the US for telemetry etc — that's a concern.
[01:45] Priya Nair: Yep, telemetry and logs. We need to know what leaves, where logs live, and whether audit logs include unhashed prompts.
[01:52] Marco Silva: Fair. For Redwood Hosted we do have regional hosting and can restrict models to EU regions; however some control plane metadata may flow to our control plane unless you pick Dedicated or Private. We can provide a DPA and list of subprocessors. We also support host-based redaction for logs and an opt-in for storing minimal logs.
[02:06] Daniel Park: Can you confirm whether Hosted has the option to use customer-managed keys? That's a dealbreaker for us on certain data sets.
[02:13] Avery Chen: Customer-managed keys (CMK) are available for Dedicated and Private today. Hosted — we're piloting BYOK for enterprise accounts but it's not generally available as CMK for all hosted customers.
[02:22] Maya Iqbal: So CMK only on Dedicated/Private. That nudges us toward those. But we need to understand cost delta and operational responsibilities.
[02:29] Marco Silva: Right. Dedicated gives you dedicated GPU pools in a region you specify, plus the option to use your KMS via a cloud integration or bring your own HSM in Private. We'll share our typical cost bands.
[02:40] Sara Whitman: On logging: regulator requires both decision logs and a way to produce a human-readable trail. We can't retain raw PII beyond masked form. Can Redwood redact on ingest?
[02:50] Marco Silva: We support pre-ingest redaction rules and also post-processing retention policies. Practical caveat: if you redact the prompt before sending to model you lose some ability to debug model outputs. Some customers prefer pseudonymization with reversible token mapping stored in their vault.
[03:06] Tom Ruiz: Reversible mapping would require us to manage the mapping securely — doesn't sound bad, as long as we can control the keys.
[03:12] Maya Iqbal: Reversible tokenization is sensitive; if it's stored by a vendor we need legal assurances.
[03:18] Daniel Park: I want to flag requests around e-discovery and legal hold. If there's litigation, sometimes we need to preserve certain logs in their original form. How flexible is your retention and legal-hold support?
[03:28] Marco Silva: We can preserve snapshots for legal hold in Dedicated/Private. Hosted has policy-based retention but legal hold flexibility is more limited. We can export immutable snapshots to your S3 if needed.
[03:38] Priya Nair: From an architecture view — for Private (VPC) we can deploy our control plane partially in your VPC and have inference nodes on-prem or in your cloud account. That gives you audit logs and KMS locally.
[03:49] Sara Whitman: Does that require opening ports to Redwood or do you run entirely inside our VPC?
[03:54] Marco Silva: Private can be customer-hosted (we ship a package you install) or a VPC peering model where the data plane sits in your VPC and control signals are over a secured channel. There are multiple patterns depending on your compliance posture.
[04:05] Tom Ruiz: Latency — advisor UX is sensitive. If we route EU traffic to a private cluster in eu-west-1, what's the latency profile?
[04:12] Priya Nair: Also need to balance latency vs cost and maintenance.
[04:16] Marco Silva: If you pin to eu-west-1 with local GPU nodes, typical 1–2 token latencies are comparable to public cloud endpoints — we can share benchmark numbers. Dedicated gives predictable tail latency; Private depends on your infra.
[04:28] Sara Whitman: What about SOC2 and penetration testing reports?
[04:32] Avery Chen: We'll send SOC2 Type II, pen test summary, and our DPA. For Dedicated/Private we can provide more detailed architecture docs.
[04:39] Daniel Park: On DPA: we expect subprocessors list, data flow diagrams, liabilities tied to data breach and cross-border transfer mechanisms (SCCs, UK addendum). Do you support SCCs?
[04:50] Avery Chen: Yes, we support standard SCCs and UK addendum. For Private deployments we can avoid cross-border transfers entirely if deployed in-region.
[04:58] Maya Iqbal: HIPAA — a small part of our use has employee medical benefits info for advisor scheduling. It's borderline, but we might require HIPAA controls for that workload. Can Redwood cover HIPAA BAA?
[05:10] Marco Silva: Redwood supports HIPAA for Dedicated and Private customers with BAAs. Hosted HIPAA support is limited and requires an enterprise plan. We'll confirm in the security pack.
[05:20] Tom Ruiz: Do audit logs include the KV cache or internal model state? We must ensure those aren't persisted with PII.
[05:27] Marco Silva: Internal KV cache is ephemeral and never written to persistent logs in our standard configurations. Logs are request/response and system metrics. We can configure to never persist full prompts or to store hashed prompts only.
[05:38] Sara Whitman: Hashing is interesting but regulator will want deterministic mapping for replay sometimes. They want to be able to link back decisions to original inputs.
[05:46] Maya Iqbal: Which is why pseudonymization with reversible mapping stored by us works better.
[05:50] Avery Chen: We'll note that and propose patterns — redaction, reversible pseudonymization under your key, or full private deployment.
[05:57] Daniel Park: Pricing question: if we choose Dedicated in eu-west-1 with CMK and log retention for seven years, how do we estimate costs?
[06:05] Marco Silva: Cost components: reserved GPU capacity (monthly commit), storage for logs (S3 or equivalent), retention and snapshot storage, and engineering/integration time for private keys. We'll send a sample spreadsheet.
[06:14] Sara Whitman: On the subject of retention and egress — can logs be routed to our S3 in EU only? We want all logs under our control.
[06:22] Marco Silva: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we can stream logs to your EU S3 bucket. Hosted supports log export but may transit our control plane unless configured with VPC endpoints.
[06:32] Priya Nair: Let's talk about sample data types. Tom, can you summarize typical prompt examples and QPS?
[06:37] Tom Ruiz: We're expecting bursts during market open, single-digit qps per advisor but high concurrency when we run overnight batch scoring — maybe 200 qps for batch windows. Payload sizes vary — short prompts (<1 KB) for recommendations, longer context for KYC items (2–6 KB).
[06:52] Marco Silva: Good to know. Batching and KV caching help with batch windows to save cost. We'll show quantization and batching options.
[06:58] Sara Whitman: On encryption at rest — do you offer encryption with our CMK covering logs and model cache?
[07:04] Marco Silva: With Dedicated/Private, yes, you can wrap volume and object storage keys with your CMK. Hosted we manage keys by default but offer some enterprise BYOK options.
[07:13] Daniel Park: On subprocessor transparency — we need an up-to-date list and notification window for new subprocessors.
[07:19] Avery Chen: We'll provide subprocessor list and commit to 30-day notice for changes, and we can put that in the contract.
[07:26] Maya Iqbal: Any data residency gotchas — backups, analytics, or telemetry? Where do those go?
[07:33] Marco Silva: By default telemetry aggregates to our analytics stack; for Dedicated/Private you can opt out and send telemetry to your endpoint. We'll highlight which features cause cross-region metadata flows.
[07:44] Tom Ruiz: What about anonymized usage data for model improvement — do you use customer prompts to train models?
[07:50] Priya Nair: Most vendors have opt-in/out for model training.
[07:53] Avery Chen: Redwood does not train public models on customer prompts by default. We have a strict policy, and training with customer data is opt-in and subject to contract. We'll include the privacy policy language.
[08:02] Daniel Park: Ok good. We need clarity on that for legal.
[08:06] Sara Whitman: How do you handle role-based access for logs and prompts? We need RBAC with least privilege, and ability to revoke quickly.
[08:14] Marco Silva: We support RBAC and SSO (SAML/OIDC). For Private deployments, you can map to your internal IAM and audit. We'll share role examples.
[08:23] Maya Iqbal: Are admin access requests logged and alerted? We need to detect suspicious access to replay or unredacted logs.
[08:30] Marco Silva: Yes — admin actions are logged with an immutable audit trail. We can configure alerts to your SIEM.
[08:36] Tom Ruiz: Any SOC2 / pen test caveats we should know about? E.g., do you run third-party pentests on private deployments?
[08:43] Marco Silva: For hosted and dedicated we run regular third-party pentests. For private customer-hosted packages, you can run your own pen tests and we have a process to coordinate.
[08:52] Priya Nair: Before we go further, any dealbreakers from your side?
[08:55] Sara Whitman: If Hosted requires any US-only telemetry or we can't control keys for EU PII, that's a dealbreaker for advisor flows.
[09:03] Daniel Park: For HIPAA pieces we probably require a BAA and prefer Dedicated/Private.
[09:08] Avery Chen: Understood. We're hearing a preference for Dedicated or Private. We'll prioritize the detailed architecture and security pack.
[09:15] Maya Iqbal: A couple of clarifying Qs — do you support field-level redaction or only full-prompt redaction?
[09:22] Marco Silva: We support both. Field-level via JSON schema is possible (you define fields to strip/mask); prompt-level redaction is also available. Field-level keeps structure for downstream tooling.
[09:31] Sara Whitman: Good — we want to keep structured logs for analytics.
[09:35] Tom Ruiz: Can you give an example of reversible pseudonymization flows? How is mapping stored?
[09:41] Marco Silva: Typical flow: you tokenize PII at ingest with a reversible cipher using your key; token mapping is stored in your vault (not Redwood's) or in a customer-held S3. Redwood can call your vault for re-identification only when you authorize it.
[09:55] Daniel Park: That architecture sounds promising — but we need contractual guarantees for mapping storage and access controls.
[10:01] Avery Chen: We'll include recommended contractual language in the security pack.
[10:05] Priya Nair: From ops — how long does it take to spin up Dedicated in eu-west-1 if we sign a 6–12 month commit?
[10:12] Marco Silva: Provisioning typically 2–4 weeks for basic Dedicated. Private install varies depending on on-prem networking. We'll put a project plan in the SE deep dive.
[10:22] Sara Whitman: For pilot success criteria — we care about latency percentiles, cost per request, and ability to demonstrate audit traceability without exposing PII.
[10:31] Avery Chen: Great. We'll propose pilot metrics: p95 latency under X ms, end-to-end cost estimate, and sample audit export containing masked prompts and mapping flow.
[10:41] Maya Iqbal: Can we get a copy of your standard BAA language?
[10:46] Avery Chen: Yes — included in the docs we'll send.
[10:49] Marco Silva: I'll also attach an architecture diagram of the VPC peering pattern and a sample log redaction config example in the follow-up.
[10:58] Tom Ruiz: For batch scoring, does Redwood support token streaming or do we need parallel requests?
[11:03] Priya Nair: There's batching vs streaming tradeoffs.
[11:06] Marco Silva: We support both. Batch windows can be optimized with continuous batching and KV caches to reduce cost. We'll map that to your QPS profile.
[11:15] Sara Whitman: Anything else on compliance — encryption in transit? FIPS?
[11:20] Marco Silva: TLS 1.2+ everywhere. For FIPS/HSM we can discuss HSM-backed keys in Private. We'll include details.
[11:28] Daniel Park: We also need to know your SLA for data availability and retention tamper detect.
[11:34] Avery Chen: SLA varies by plan; Dedicated/Private have stronger SLAs. We'll include uptime, RPO/RTO guidance, and retention/tamper controls in the security pack.
[11:45] Maya Iqbal: On data subject requests (DSRs) under GDPR — can we perform search and deletion?
[11:51] Marco Silva: Yes — for Dedicated/Private you can run deletion workflows; for Hosted we have APIs for DSRs but deletion timelines may vary. We'll show the API.
[12:02] Sara Whitman: One last question — any limitations on model variants for in-region hosting? Some large models have vendor restrictions.
[12:09] Marco Silva: Some upstream models have export restrictions; we'll surface model availability per region in the catalog. We also have Redwood-verified lightweight variants for low-latency in-region needs.
[12:20] Avery Chen: OK — recap and next steps: we'll send security pack (DPA, SOC2, pen test summary, BAA draft), VPC/Private architecture doc, cost spreadsheet for Dedicated in eu-west-1 with retention, and schedule a follow-up SE deep dive next week. Action items captured in the notes.
[12:38] Daniel Park: Thanks everyone, that helps. We'll review and loop in procurement if costs look reasonable.
[12:43] Maya Iqbal: Appreciate the thoroughness.
[12:45] Sara Whitman: Thanks — talk soon.
[12:47] Avery Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the docs and a Doodle for the deep dive.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hears of acronyms (e.g., KV cache transcribed as 'K V cash' sometimes), timestamps approximate. Some speaker labels may be generic in the auto transcription.
